title: Human Brain Anatomy: Lobes, Ventricles & Neural Pathway
description: Discover human brain anatomy across all four cerebral lobes, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, brainstem, and ventricular fluid systems.
h1: Human Brain Anatomy: Cerebral Lobes, Deep Nuclei and Pathways
blurb: Folded cerebral lobes, white-matter commissures, deep thalamic and basal nuclei, cerebellum, and brainstem circuits floating in protective cerebrospinal fluid.
lead: Weighing about 1.4 kilograms yet consuming nearly a fifth of the body's oxygen, the human brain weaves billions of neurons into folded cortex and deep relay nuclei. In this illustrated guide to human brain anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including cerebrum, frontal lobe, parietal lobe, occipital lobe—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Weighing about 1.4 kilograms yet consuming nearly a fifth of the body's oxygen, the human brain weaves billions of neurons into folded cortex and deep relay nuclei. The brain integrates sensation, generates movement, and supports language, memory and consciousness. It uses about 20% of the body's oxygen and glucose despite being 2% of body weight, and it has almost no energy reserve — four minutes of ischaemia starts to kill neurons. The cerebral cortex is folded into gyri and sulci to pack ~0.15 m² of grey matter into the skull. Beneath it, white-matter tracts such as the corpus callosum connect the hemispheres, while the diencephalon and brainstem handle relay, arousal and the automatic control of breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Within the human body, the brain (Encephalon) is situated in cranial cavity, above the brainstem, receives arterial perfusion via internal carotid + vertebral arteries → circle of Willis (15% of cardiac output), and serves directly as the origin of cranial nerves I–XII.

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain: two hemispheres of folded cortex over deep white matter, basal ganglia and the lateral ventricles. Physiologically, the cerebrum governs voluntary movement, sensation, language, memory, personality and conscious thought. The frontal lobe (Lobus frontalis) is anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex. Physiologically, the frontal lobe governs planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech. Anatomically, the parietal lobe (Lobus parietalis) lies behind the central sulcus, above the temporal lobe. Houses the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus. Physiologically, the parietal lobe governs processing of touch, pain, temperature, position sense and spatial awareness. The occipital lobe (Lobus occipitalis) is the posterior pole, bounded medially by the parieto-occipital sulcus, containing the primary visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. Physiologically, the occipital lobe governs vision — the retinal image is mapped point-for-point on the calcarine cortex. Anatomically, the temporal lobe (Lobus temporalis) lies below the lateral sulcus, including the hippocampal formation and primary auditory cortex on the superior temporal gyrus. Physiologically, the temporal lobe governs hearing, memory formation, language comprehension (Wernicke's area) and emotion. The corpus callosum is the great C-shaped commissure of ~200 million myelinated fibres: rostrum, genu, body and splenium. Physiologically, the corpus callosum connects matching regions of the two hemispheres so they work as one brain.

Clinically, regarding the cerebrum, its surface folding (gyri and sulci) triples cortical area; abnormal folding causes lissencephaly and epilepsy. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the frontal lobe, prefrontal damage (classically Phineas Gage) changes personality and impulse control while sparing memory and IQ. In clinical pathology involving the parietal lobe, right-sided lesions cause hemispatial neglect — the patient ignores the whole left side of space. Medical evaluation of the occipital lobe also notes that a posterior cerebral artery stroke causes a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

questions.question: What are the main parts of the brain?
questions.answer: The cerebrum supports complex thought, sensation and voluntary movement; the cerebellum coordinates movement; and the brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord and helps regulate essential functions. Physiologically, the cerebrum governs voluntary movement, sensation, language, memory, personality and conscious thought.

questions.question: What protects the brain inside the skull?
questions.answer: The skull, three meningeal layers and cerebrospinal fluid provide physical protection. Blood vessels supply its metabolically active tissue. The corpus callosum is the great C-shaped commissure of ~200 million myelinated fibres: rostrum, genu, body and splenium. Physiologically, the corpus callosum connects matching regions of the two hemispheres so they work as one brain.

questions.question: What is the frontal lobe?
questions.answer: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex. Functionally, it governs planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech. In clinical pathology involving the frontal lobe, prefrontal damage (classically Phineas Gage) changes personality and impulse control while sparing memory and IQ.

questions.question: Where is the thalamus located?
questions.answer: Two ovals of grey matter flanking the third ventricle, subdivided into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. Functionally, it serves as the relay station: nearly all sensory information (except smell) is edited and sent on to the cortex. Also involved in arousal. Medical evaluation of the thalamus also notes that a thalamic stroke can produce severe contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.

questions.question: What is the function of the cerebellum?
questions.answer: Functionally, it compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects it: coordination, precision, timing, posture and motor learning. Two hemispheres and a midline vermis, with a densely folded cortex, deep nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) and branching white matter — the arbor vitae. Clinically, regarding the cerebellum, damage causes ipsilateral ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and a broad-based gait. Alcohol affects it first.
